subject: science
objective: Use evidence from continent shapes, fossils, rocks, glacier marks, and magnetic stripes on the ocean floor to explain that Earth's lithosphere is broken into plates that move a few centimeters a year; calculate a spreading rate from distance and age; and identify divergent, convergent (ocean-continent, ocean-ocean, continent-continent), and transform boundaries from the landforms, earthquakes, and volcanoes each one produces.
prerequisites: Earth has layers: crust, mantle, and core
Fossils are preserved remains of living things
sources: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics (https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/dynamic.html)
NOAA Ocean Exploration, What is the mid-ocean ridge? (https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/facts/mid-ocean-ridge.html)
Ogg, J. G. (2020). Geomagnetic Polarity Time Scale. In Gradstein et al. (eds.), Geologic Time Scale 2020, Elsevier, for reversal ages back to 3.6 million years
misconceptions: Plates float on a layer of melted rock or lava
Continents plow through the ocean floor on their own
Plates move only during earthquakes, or move fast enough to notice
Plate boundaries are the same as coastlines
New crust at ridges means Earth is getting bigger
All volcanoes are at plate boundaries
The ocean floor is as old as the continents
Mountains only exist where plates meet today
modelLimitations: Continent outlines are hand-simplified and drawn on a flat longitude-latitude grid; the fit is a two-dimensional turn and slide chosen to match ten pairs of coastal points, not a reconstruction on a sphere.
Clue areas (fossils, ancient rocks, glacier deposits) are approximate outlines simplified from published maps.
The drift slider moves Africa in a straight line at a steady rate; the real motion curved and changed speed.
The seafloor spreading view shows straight, sharp-edged magnetic bands; real ridges are offset by transform faults, bands are wavy, and reversals take thousands of years.
Reversal ages are rounded to 0.01 million years. Spreading speeds are representative (2.5 and 15 cm per year in total), not measurements of a specific profile.
Cross-sections are not to scale. Depths are stretched relative to widths, the asthenosphere boundary is drawn as a sharp line, and plates move evenly instead of in stick-slip steps.
Melting above sinking plates is shown at one spot; in reality it happens over a zone, and magma takes complicated paths to the surface.
The transform fault uses a simple stick-slip model with equal-sized earthquakes at regular intervals; real earthquakes vary in size and timing.
Boundary detective cases simplify real places that can involve more than one process (for example, Iceland is both a ridge and a hot spot).
